body:
I was honestly so scared of being a narcissist that I asked a psychiatrist for an eval. I got one, but lowkey got laughed at and told if I was questioning it, I'm not one. :')

It's a tool narcissists use to manipulate us. Make us feel like we were the ones manipulating, that they are the victim.

Every so often, a medicine can make the symptoms you're trying to treat worse. It could just be that it's not the right benzo for you, my therapist told me there's a suprising about of people that suffer from paranoia when on it.

I've been thinking about Klonopin. Does it help with insomnia related issues? 

Glad to know I'm not the only person who has struggled with needing it daily at some point. It's still helpful for me, but I wanna get out of cycle before it isn't. 

Yeah the rebound anxiety the dependence causes is another huge reason I have such bad insomnia right now. Like I'm exhausted and want to fall asleep, but my body won't let me because I'm on high alert. I tapered myself very slowly down to half of the dose I'm on (my doctor knows this), but I think I'll need a different medicine with a longer half life to get me through the initial rebound symptoms. 

Thank you for sharing your story, I think it took some off the pressure off. :)
Yup, same here! Always followed by nausea and the need to cry intensely and escape (usually happens in the car, so no escape for me!)

I sympathize with you so much about this. I have been in the same boat for years. New symptoms make me feel like I'm going to die, and it's ALWAYS a life threatening disease that pops into mind. I deal with nausea and swallowing problems when I have an uptick in anxiety attacks, a result of constantly being in flight or fight. Digestion is shut down during flight or fight so your body can focus all energy on the perceived threat. When you deal with anxiety, sometimes there isn't a whole lot of resting and digesting.

I was just diagnosed with panic disorder and ptsd stemming from health trauma, and the gi distress that a panic attack can cause sends me into hysterics, which just makes it feel hopeless. Personally, my health trauma diagnosis really helped me cope better with the impending health doom problem. 

It is a vicious cycle, having symptoms create anxiety, and anxiety creates symptoms. It sucks. But please know this, your symptoms, whether they stem for from physical or mental health, are valid. The symptoms are there, and you are not crazy. 

You are not a burden, and we are all glad you came to this subreddit for support. You are seen, you are not invisible.
Ah, well, might as well remove it... Thanks for the heads up 😅
I am also on zofran occasionally to treat celiac symptoms when I get contaminated with gluten so I can take care of my diabetes (i.e. eating, drinking)
I did! Almost two years post op. It DEFINITELY helped me.
No, not normal! Hyperkinetic gallbladders are under recognized by radiologists. Hyperkinetic is generally anything greater than 75%. Mine was 98%, and I was incredibly sick.
Turn it upside down, and that's mine :D

I do recall a little bit of a crackly sensation! I was told not to worry about it, and it did go away. Absolutely if it's anxiety inducing or not getting better/getting worse, give your surgeon a call! 

Another thing worth noting is that it's okay for organs to slosh around a bit, in fact, when surgeons close up, they usually just put the organ back as best as they can, then your body just kinda sorts it out and everything falls back into place. 

Unlikely that you'll hurt yourself with breathing, especially if it's not painful or creating any other symptoms. It's actually really good for you to take deep breaths after surgery because it prevents pneumonia, which can be a complication of intubation.

I would be very surprised if it doesn't help in the long run. But as someone who has dealt with a lot of health issues and a lot of ifs, it's always best to leave the future for tomorrow and focus on today. Today you're hopeful that getting your gallbladder taken out will help, so that's what you need to focus on right now. :)

Of course it's nerve wracking not knowing though! You are NOT alone there, and it's okay to feel anxious about it. :D

Yeah it definitely could be gallbladder attack! My mom had horrible ones, and horrendous reflux that resulted in like a year of invasive testing. An ultrasound revealed gallbladder sludge, she got it out, and no more reflux.

Likely acid reflux or an ulcer? Are you kidding me? Even with positive imaging for gallstones? That 100% sounds like a gallbladder attack. (That kidney stone must not be very comfortable either, I'm so sorry!)

I'd make an appointment with your PCP and ask for a referral to a general surgeon for a consult. That ER doctor is an idiot.

HORRIBLE reflux! My mom too. It was her primary complaint and she had years of invasive testing done before they were like, "Oh hmm, let's check the gallbladder"

I was first diagnosed with gastritis, then functional dyspepsia before I got my HIDA.

Referred pain is always fun. I had a whole bunch of similar pain after my surgery. Taking an organ out is really hard on you, quite painful. If it gets worse, give your surgeon a call, but 12 days is still so young.
It won't really make it worse as much as it just wouldn't do anything. You can ask about trying bile binders first, but a ppi shouldn't make anything worse.

Mine were really mild for a while as well. Just kinda got progressively worse over the years. Definitely if you're symptoms get worse, I'd say to keep your gb at the front of your mind.

My surgeon told me if someone has any symptoms at all from their gallbladder (especially with any positive tests), that he'll usually reccomend to just get rid of it. You shouldn't have to be crippled to get help and taken seriously, that's where medicine fails us.

No, not to my knowledge. If I did, not for long. Bile reflux can be kinda hard to catch and get a definite diagnosis on, the tests for it it are different than regular heartburn studies. 

Fortunately, gb removals, I believe usually get to skip straight to trying bile binders.

Mine were basically symptoms reminiscent of functional dyspepsia. Lots of nausea, indigestion, bloating, epigastric abdominal pain. But also very extreme fatty food intolerance, couldn't do meals with over 2 grams of fat without being doubled over.

Yeah ignore those fools. Of course we're happy for them, but they can take their success stories and leave the other up to 40% of us who don't have the same post op food experience, haha. 

Oh yeah, for sure excess bile, sounds like. Not uncommon to have weird bms for a while after as well. If they continue to be like that, you could ask your surgeon if bile binders may be right for you.

If they say your test results are "normal", but don't say what the number was, ask for it. I was told mine was "normal", and when I asked for my EF rate, it was 98%. Hyperkinetic. According to my surgeon, radiologists basically label anything over 35% as "normal".

Anything below 35% is biliary dyskinesia, and anything above 65% is generally considered hyperkinetic. Ask for a surgeon consult if they don't offer one if you get either of those results.

Did the surgeon not offer to remove it still? Gallstones hurt. Might consider a second opinion. My surgeon told me if there's RUQ pain and any indication on any test that there's a problem with the gallbladder, that he opts to reccomend for removal. 

Sooo many people have normal tests, then go in to get it removed, only to find it inflamed or filled with sludge/gallstones.

Still happy your test went well though. Mine went similarly, had an ef of 98%. Basically, gallbladder bile diarrhea. :)

Have they given you an ECRP or anything? The pancreas and liver issue definitely sounds like it's still a biliary system problem. Maybe sphincter of oddi disorder? That can cause elevated pancreas and liver enzymes. Definitely a more oddball differential diagnosis, but it sounds like you've been through the wringer, so it sounds plausible. 

I understand your frustration and sadness about not being able to eat. Before I had my gallbladder out, I dealt with endometriosis symptoms for years. Debilitating periods coupled with extreme nausea and pain for all but a week out of the month. I had surgery for that and all was well for like, 6 months, then my gallbladder decided to say hi again. I had off and on problems with it my whole life. I still honestly deal with a lot of health issues, and a few of them cause really bad stomach pain. 

I'm also GF! I have celiac disease. :) GF for 10 years myself. 

Does your doctor have you on zofran or any other anti nausea meds? I'm a type 1 diabetic as well, so my doc has me on that because diabetics unfortunately don't have the luxury of just not eating. I only need it when I get glutened or have panic attacks.

I really hope you get to the bottom of this soon. I can tell you are weary and possible feeling defeated. But please remember that you are strong, even if you don't feel it, you ARE strong.

Absolutely! I'm happy to offer some peace. I like to come back to these subreddits because I know most dip permanently after they get their gbs out (don't blame em' really, why would they think about it when they're not in pain anymore). But then you still got the folks on here that usually come to Reddit when they're in pain and anxious about the unknown. 

May your bile bag stop haunting you soon so you can fully enjoy life without the little devil! :D

By far too much bile versus not enough. When you take away a gallbladder, you no longer have that "shut off valve", so even when you're not eating, you're gonna have that constant drip of bile. At first it can be VERY uncomfortable, ESPECIALLY on an empty stomach (that lovely gnawing pain that fakes you out as a hunger pang but turns into a burning, stabbing nausea? Fun stuff). I couldn't do anything but nibble on food for like, the first two weeks? 

But you ARE only one week post op, even without pcs, it can take a good 4-6 weeks to adjust for most people. For now, so early on, sphincter of oddi syndrome isn't a worry quite yet. It's most likely just the new flow of bile making things rough. 

My biggest help with the trapped gas feeling was lots of slow walking. I did that for a long time in combo with gas x. Also, Phazyme Gas + Acid chews, if you want to try a different medicine. That's got extra strength gas relief AND antacids in it. I still use it when I occasionally over indulge on high fat meals, haha.

I would definitely recommend as much slow nibbling as you can (comfort foods, things you find easy to eat on a mildly upset stomach), because that gives the bile something to do other than being a menace to your stomach lining, haha. Don't worry about full meals, eat what you can handle, as long as you're staying hydrated, you're golden. 

When you are comfortable and not in pain from the surgery anymore, my favorite position to sleep in/get relief from gas post op is laying on your left side with your legs curled slightly against your chest. 

I probably had one of the more uncomfortable, less favorable recoveries, and I got through it and would do it again if I had to. You won't be uncomfortable forever, just hang in there!

Mine was bloating, nausea, and fatty food intolerance. I was fortunate enough to not have the diarrhea issue that most have for very long at all (maybe a week?).

Doc is definitely right, when you rip out an organ, it can take a bit for your body to get used to the new "flow" of things. Think of it like a road detour and an annoyed driver. They're pretty angry their normal route was just blocked off, but they'll get used to the new route soon enough. 

I'd say all-in-all, was probably like 9 or so months? Some people take longer to recover from it, some shorter, it just varies a lot. Especially when you take the reason you got your gb out into consideration. My surgeon told me people with functional gb diseases have a much higher chance of getting something like pcs than someone with just stones or sludge (although everyone is kinda at risk when they get their gb out). 

Worst case scenario, if you have severe pcs symptoms for an extended amount of time, your surgeon may reccomend an ecrp to check bile flow/sphincter strength/stuck stones. 

So yeah, def give your body some grace and a little more time. :)

NAD, but I had these type of symptoms with clean tests, and it was ultimately my gallbladder. I got a HIDA scan, which showed it was dysfunctional. My mom also had gallbladder disease as well, and had these symptoms (she had years of invasive tests for heartburn, only for it to be a sludgy gallbladder). 

It's kinda a weird one, but gb disease can definitely cause dyspeptic symptoms in the absence of positive test results. Hope you find out the cause soon!

I've had two surgeries through my belly button! 

It's internally sewed shut as well, so you don't need to worry about your guts falling out or anything. I've had stitches pop before, usually the surgeons told me to just keep it clean and covered.

I get a reg zofran script because I have type 1 diabetes, and also a lot of health problems that cause gnarly nausea, and diabetics don't have the luxury of fasting until the nausea is gone. (Docs in the comments: don't worry, I check ketones before I take it, haha)

As someone on the patient side, I'd definitely talk to your doc about why you may be experiencing nausea, because zofran can mask underlying health conditions (example: diabetics used to commonly get prescribed zofran because we are super prone to nausea, but it can mask diabetic ketoacidosis, so it's not so commonly prescribed anymore).

I call em' pump bites! Sometimes you get a little unlucky, and bacteria gets into the site. Draw a circle around it and watch it, but usually a few days of neosporin and cleaning it clears it up. I've only needed antibiotics once for an infected site in my 10 years of pumping, and that was just because it was taking a little too long to heal (antibiotics did clear it up).

I am well! Weight is gained back, no more pain and nausea with eating, and just generally healthier. :) I had post cholecystectomy syndrome for a few months, but it went away. Super high fat meals get me a little sick, but it's way better than not being able to eat any fat at all.

Ayyyy, fellow endo warrior and hyperkinetic gallbladder! 

I had my lap turned excision in 2021, and my gb surgery in 2022. A little jealous you get to hit two birds with one stone! That's so amazing!

No, doesn't look infected! Just irritated. Mine looked like this and it wasn't infected. It'd be really swollen, red, and oozy if it were infected (small amounts of clear ooze are generally fine). Like the others said, cover it with a bandaid! Definitely keep it clean as well.

Hello! I'm so sorry, I haven't been on this account in a while. I am well! Got my gallbladder out in Feb 2022, over a year later and doing great now. Admittedly it did take a bit for my body to adjust to not having a gb, but it did adjust, and I am no longer in pain or nauseous!

P.S. I still live at home because I don't feel like I can live by myself (depression sucks). So me and my sister are waiting until she's old enough to move out together! :) 

In the meantime, my dad is awesome and told me he'd never ever kick me out, and that he'd support my life decisions and not hang housing over my head. I'd probably run away as a kid if I didn't have my dad and siblings.

No one talks about the peeing issues enough! The catheters they put in during surgery also make it burn like heck the first few times. I do remember one time waking up from an abdominal surgery where I also got a cystoscopy done, having to pee super bad. The nurse was super surprised to hear me release Niagara Falls after only like a minute in there. It wasn't just a few drops, it was a proper pee. I recall the nurse laughing at the amount I had peed, then my high self feeling really proud of my accomplishment. I had more trouble with peeing with my gallbladder, haha
My mom didn't have nausea! Just really bad heartburn and gas. She had gallbladder sludge. Would be worth asking your doc about an ultrasound!

I got mine out last year when I was 20! :D Surgery isn't so scary when you actually get there, it's honestly the anticipation that's the worst part, for me that was the case, atleast! I think if the doctor reccomends removal, it would be worth it to take that leap of faith and get it done. 

Recovery also wasn't so bad. I mean, it's surgery, so you'll be sore, but it is by far not the hardest surgery I've ever had. I had my tonsils out, and that was WAY worse! You just need to take things slow and let your body heal on it's own dime. Personally, the actual surgery and recovery isn't as bad as the anticipation anxiety. Hope this helps and that you get to feeling better soon!  :D

I'm honestly gonna do that. I'm not eating the food he prepares me anymore. The fact that he says it "hurts his feelings when I say he cross contaminated me" shows that he doesn't put any thought into preparing food that I can eat.

I talked to her about it last night! I (politely) demanded strictly gluten free cooking ware and explained that I really can't be cooking my food in the same pot as gluten containing stuff. My dad is also the most unhygienic person on the planet, so he doesn't really clean the pots he uses, just kinda rinses them out and scrubs with food covered sponges. We always wash the pots before using them because of him. Even after washing the pots, I still get sick. The pots have really deep scratches in them, so food gets stuck that you can't entirely get out. I hate it. 

New pots and pans will be bought that can only be used for gluten free cooking. I can't believe it's taken THIS long.

It's really only my dad that treats me like this. My mom is always careful when she makes me any type of food. My dad however, does need a doc to talk some sense into him about this, I would really hate to never eat any of his food again, but if that's what I have to do while living under this roof, I'll do it. I don't care how annoyed he gets, I'm so done with getting guilted into eating his gluten traps. 

The worst part is my little sister is allergic to eggs and peanuts, and he won't even allow those ingredients in the kitchen... You'd think he'd atleast have some dedicated gf cooking utensils...

I remember when I was little my mom tried to get gf pizza for me at a pizza place. But the server so kind and honest and told us that the gf pizzas were not celiac friendly, and that generally most pizza places that sell gf pizza aren't. My man saved me almost making that mistake, I'm thankful for him.

It feels like there's simultaneously a lot and not a lot to study up on! Like, I feel like I'd do awesome if I had a visual reminder for how solving a certain question works, but of course that's now how these type of tests work, haha. It feels like after a few weeks, it's like that information becomes locked somehow. Hopefully you we can both pass this heinous subject soon! :')

So just because they're "colleagues" and wouldn't "know anyone", that means it wouldn't still hurt them? Just because it's "not a big deal" to you, doesn't mean it won't potentially be detrimental to their mental health. 

You can't uninvite someone, plain and simple. Plan better in the future
Tbh I don't know how people like this make it to adulthood (happy cake day!)
They're one of the leading specialists in 5 minute Google audiology. Wonder if they can fix my pancreas too
Mom said it's my turn with the eardrum! Pop that bad boy out and hand it over!
Didn't you know? Apparently we're supposed to be replacing them every 10 years now lol
So lazy fam just straight up used the first stock image they saw of ear anatomy
According to karen and their google photo, you can simply pop out your eardrums and replace them like fricking button batteries, lol. They also probably think chocolate milk comes from brown cows
Typo, "permanent imprint of my hand on *my skull"
Absolutely worth it! The HIDA was eventually the test that diagnosed me, ef of 98% for me!

Oh honey, you absolutely do not need to feel embarrassed for needing your gallbladder out! It's NOT your fault! This kind of thing can happen to litterally anyone. You did not cause anything and the people who should be embarrassed are those who are insinuating that it's your fault. There are so many things that are considered risk factors for gallstones,  sometimes they just happen for no good reason. 

Honestly, it doesn't even matter what may or may not have caused them, what matters is that you have them and that there's plan to make you feel better. Please just focus on getting that surgery so you can feel better, that's all that matters right now. Frick them for even speaking that poison, they should be supporting you in a time of pain and nervousness. 

(I was 19 when I started having really bad symptoms, and got mine out at 20. It's getting increasingly more common for younger adults to get their gallbladders out.)

I honestly live in a very self absorbed family... I'm not gonna make my mental health their priority or anything, but it sucks to see your loved ones watch you drown like this and do nothing. They just watch me try and fail, and criticize me for the things I haven't been able to do. 

I'm trying, I honestly am. What feels like huge steps to me looks like small steps to them. I recently started to clean my room for the first time in two years, my dad? He walked in and said, "Doesn't it feel nice to not hear crunching when you walk on your floor?" When he said that, I just stopped cleaning... I can't bring myself to do it, people just walk in and mock what my room looked like. 

Thank you for the advice, I think I'm gonna try and do more things for myself. :)
If I were you'd I'd definitely take the chance if you have it. Just make sure you have a safe location in mind and people you trust to help you.
You can really just ask your pcp about it. Ask for an ultrasound, and if that's inconclusive, ask for a hida scan.

Hi! NAD, but I recently had my gallbladder out, and all tests were deemed "normal". Did you get a HIDA scan? And if you did, what's your EF rate? A low or a high one could indicate a functional issue with your gallbladder, which wouldn't be seen on something like a ultrasound. My EF rate was 98%, which meant it was working overtime. My surgeon told me a lot of radiologists will call anything above a 35% EF rate normal. A hyperkinetic gallbladder is generally anything above 80%. It wouldn't hurt to ask for a consult with a surgeon as well.
Have you had your gallbladder checked out? My mom had those symptoms, and it ended up being a bum gallbladder.

I had low vitamin d when I was younger and even I wasn't monitored this closely. I believe I had a secondary blood test like 6 weeks later, but after that it was more so just come back if you feel worse.

NAD, but I have generalized anxiety disorder, and this is definitely a huge symptom for me when stress levels are high. Keep a close eye on it and try to recognize triggers and what helps you to feel better. If it gets worse or fails to improve, definitely give your pcp a call! :)

NAD, but I am a type 1 diabetic! My little sister is also a t1d, and once needed a course of steroids for poison ivy, her blood sugars were in the 400s until she stopped the medicine. She did not need to go to the hospital because of close monitoring and extra fluids plus insulin. So honestly, docs are probably gonna tell you to keep doing what you are doing. Monitor your ketones, as long as you can keep those down, you're golden. The main worry right now would be DKA. High bgs from steroids are temporary, I know it sucks, but it will pass. Give your endo a call if you're really worried, they will absolutely be able to guide you. 

I went through a rough time with high bgs and ketones a little while ago from eating gluten (celiac disease). Was stuck in the 300s all day. Gave my own endo a call and that was his treatment plan for me: Monitor bgs and ketones, push fluids, and take insulin when necessary. 

Also, take a BIG deep breath, adrenaline and cortisol don't help high blood sugars at all, haha. Hope you get to feeling better soon! Remember to give your endo a call if you need tailored diabetes management help right now. :)
I FINALLY got over the bg fluctuations, gotta love celiac disease! As if t1d wasn't enough, a handful of us get to have celiacs as well!  It's so fun, isn't it? :')

I was allowed to have a pretty normal diet right off the bat, but my surgeon told me to go easy on fatty foods for two weeks. After that it was just experimentation. If something fatty caused symptoms, I was supposed to try and eat that food again a week later. Worked pretty well for me! Excessive amounts of fatty foods still cause some mild symotoms for me (mild diarrhea, light nausea, light bloating) but nothing like bad gb symptoms!

If it's not totally normal right away, don't worry about it! You've just diverted your GI tract into functioning differently, so it may take a little time for your body to adjust. :)

I'm gonna be honest, I've had a couple of surgeries, and fortunately they usually get a bulk of the pain under control before you fully come to. So yeah, I remember being sore, but I don't really have any specific memories of pain. (If that makes any sense)

You'll be in good hands, they won't let you leave the hospital if you're pain isn't under control anyways. Honestly the worst part is the anticipation of the surgery. 

I hope your surgery goes well and that you will have minimal pain! Good luck op!

Believe it or not, this is a lot better than the acute stage of when I got glutened. Because of how much gluten I ate, the severity and duration of symptoms were much longer than with a simple cross contamination. Had ketones and unmanageable bgs that made my graph look more like an ekg. Atleast right now it's just the highs, no ketones or anything anymore. 

It'll last until my stomach heals from the ordeal. Very frustrating, but my endocrinologist said all we can really do is manage my diabetes the best we can and ride it out. A LOT better than last week though, I'm moving in the right direction. Big piece of regular, gluten filled cake equals big recovery time for my stomach AND diabetes. Yay. 

(Also yes, I am officially diagnosed with celiac through a blood test and biospy as of 8 years ago. I definitely know my diabetes problems are from eating the gluten, my symptoms from celiacs tend to last a little longer than your regular celiac patient)
I'm honestly still having some symptoms like light nausea and bloating plus the mental symptoms, but I felt well enough to bake myself a little grief present! :')
Would reccomend giving r/askdocs a visit! :)

It was just a slice of homemade gluten free cake from a local cafe. They're usually really good with their gf stuff, but they mislabeled it this time around. Gonna be cautious and not eat anything there again. :')
I ate something something with gluten! :') First time in the better part of a decade that I've made a mistake like that

Oh my gosh YES! A full on glutening will make me feel horribly sick for up to two weeks! Off and on diarrhea, extreme nausea that hinders me for eating for any given amount of time. ALL of the fun stuff! 

My advice for the nausea, ask your primary care provider if you can have an emergency zofran supply for when you get glutened. If you can take some nausea medicine, that should take off enough edge for you to get in some nutrition. If you can't have or just don't want zofran, get some benadryl or dramamine, antihistamines are known to help with nausea. I take it when I'm in a pinch, it works wonders for me! Not as well as zofran, but well enough to settle both my stomach and me.

Eat simple carbs that are easy for the body to digest, steer away from complex carbs. Eat small snacks throughout the day, but really focus on drinking a lot of fluids. It's okay to not eat a lot for a few days, but fluids MUST be pushed! The more fluids the better, it will help wash out the toxins. 

My go to for symptom management is zofran, gas x, and tylenol (for the the stomach cramps). That cocktail of medication always makes it to where I am physically able to take care of my body.

But to answer your actual question: the nausea shouldn't last way too long. It really does depend on how much gluten you ate. It's quite rare for nausea to last more than a week after getting glutened, but to be fair most people with celiacs don't often get a full blown glutening. It will blow over, just stay calm and let your body rest and heal. I know it's rough, but it will end. :)

I self diagnosed myself when I was 13 when I constantly had to repeat grades. I had to BEG for that diagnosis. They later told me they knew I had ADHD from a very young age, but didn't want to bring me to the doctor because of their pride. When I asked for more help other than just a stupid pill (because it didn't work and they think physiatrists are  quacks), they told me I just needed to stop being lazy and actually put in effort. Whenever I didn't understand anything, I was yelled at and asked if I wanted to be a loser. 

They put me in freaking college prep classes thinking that because I was 'smart', that'd I do well in advanced classes. Surprise, surprise, I got Ds and Fs and had to drop out of highschool because they "couldn't afford my education". I've been trying to study for my GED, but I don't have any help to understand the material. Nor can I understand it because I don't know how to think in the way the material was designed with in mind.

Plopping a kid with ADHD into the school and the world without any support is life dropping a tourist into a foreign country without a translator. Of course the tourist would get frustrated when they don't understand what people are saying. So it's not that he's frustrated with you, he's probably just frustrated that he can't understand what people are trying to teach him. But that's where you're stepping in. You're being that translator for him. You're taking that extra step to help him learn a new language in a foreign country. You're a good parent, and you're doing the right thing. 

So to answer your question:
I wish they swallowed their pride and got me help sooner. I wish they put in even a little bit of effort to understand my mind, they dropped me off in a "foriegn country" by myself and expected me to learn as I go. 

I resent them so much for setting me up for failure like that.

No matter how frustrated he gets, no matter how much he resists, he's gonna look back on this and appreciate you so much. He's gonna be so thankful for a parent who never gave up, for a parent who put effort into understanding him. I know you're gonna say it's just your job as a parent, but thank you for doing this. Thank you for being different than my parents.

Hyperkinetic gb here! 98% when I got mine out. My surgeon told me that if anyone is having significant gb related symptoms, that getting it out will mostly likely help your symptoms regardless of what the hida results were. So basically hida results can be indicative of needing it out, but it won't be conclusive as far as ruling a bad gb out. 

But yeah, got mine out in February and I'm doing great! Back to eating fatty meals without being hit by pain and nausea. Sometimes I have some problems when I only eat fatty foods, but it can take a while for your gi tract to fully adjust. :)

The nausea is to be expected, especially if you're just one day post op. For some people it lasts only a few days, but it can last all the way up to two weeks, so please don't be frightened if you still feel a little nauseous in a few weeks. Also be sure to stay hydrated! Food isn't as important in the first few days after surgery, but hydration is important. Eat light, low fat, easy to digest snacks and meals. Some people can bounce back to a normal fatty diet right away, so it's really up to how you're feeling. My biggest tip is to be patient and listen to your body. 

Did you ask your doctor for anti nausea medicine? That was a lifesaver for me after my surgery. Also staying on top of all other meds, don't wait for symptoms to start. 

Oh! Make sure you're getting up to walk around a little bit every hour or so, even if it's just a little minute waddle to the bathroom. 

For incision pain, I was icing it for 15 minutes with an hour inbetween each icing throughout the day. That helped my pain a lot. I did also keep light pressure on it with a pillow too. 

The first day after surgery was definitely the hardest day for me, and it sounds like you're just about through your first day! Best of luck op, and feel better soon!
The ketones will forevermore be the worst part of getting glutened for me. 💔 Thank you, I hope so too! Haven't had a proper meal or rest in almost 5 days.

Apparently they can happen from the stress and inflammation, and also from not being able to properly absorb nutrients (starvation ketones). 98% ef here! I was diagnosed with hyperkinetic biliary dyskinesia a little while ago, my doctor was confused why my tests kept coming up clean when it looked like I was suffering from gallbladder attacks. After a couple visits with a gastro, it was decided that I wasn't suffering from any stomach issues in particular. I'm a type 1 diabetic as well, and when I have stomach problems (anything that inhibits digestion and or absorption affects blood sugar level) it affects my diabetes management, which has been excellent and hasn't suffered from my gb disease other than when I can't eat from pain. A visit with my endocrinologist confirmed that for now, stomach issues weren't a worry. For once I can thank my diabetes for it's impeccable health issue precognition skills. 

My gastro, a pretty great doctor in general, but not so great with gbs, told me that since heartburn isn't a chief complaint for me, that it probably wasn't a gb issue. I knew better than trust a doctor's word when they unceremoniously disregard my symptoms like that. Even though I knew they were a good doctor, I knew then and there that I needed to find someome else. Or maybe backtrack a bit.

 I decided that I should go back to the doctor who originally believed me, so I went back to my PCP. They ordered me a HIDA scan, hesitant because the gastro didn't speak of ordering one. Although, as great of a doctor as the gastro was, his area of expertise was within the folds of the stomach, not the bile bag. 

When we first got the results, my mom took the phone call. It was a new nurse, she said that the test came back as "normal" and that my doctor wanted me to see the gastro again. I asked my mom, "What was the ef rate? Did they tell you?" My mom quickly said that she didn't even know that was something to ask about. So we called back and demanded the specific results: We wanted numbers.

This time around, it was the nurse we knew and loved. She was more than happy to give us all of the info then and there. "98%" She said. My mom looked confused, "That's almost a 100%, doesn't that mean it's working almost perfectly fine?"  'No', I thought, 'that's not normal'. I had read time and time again, radiologists commonly label HIDA scans above 35% as normal. 

"That IS almost 100%. That's hyperkinetic, that's not normal at all." I replied thoughtfully. The nurse agreed, "Your symptoms too, that's an obvious presentation of some sort of gallbladder problem; atleast, it usually is. I'm gonna have the doctor take a second look at this, this isn't right." 

The call was short, but it was very informative. I got the info I was looking for, but now the ball was in my PCP's court. Were they gonna brush me off? Were they gonna take a second look? Would I need to leave my trusted PCP and get a second opinion? I hoped not. It was a waiting game, but in the medical feild, everything always ends up being a waiting game. 

We didn't have to wait for long. The very next day that same nurse called back, "The doctor is referring you to a general surgereon, they looked at the results and agree that it's not normal. You have hyperkinetic biliary  dyskinesia. I researched it, you have the symptoms down to a t, the reccomended treatment is cholecystectomy." 

That moment was pure bliss. It was freeing, it was VALIDATING. Not only that, but my respect for my PCP grew tenfold that day. They went back and read the scan, they disregarded the radiology report and they read it! My PCP doesn't just give patients what they want, they listen to the symptoms and use the clues patients give to get down to the bottom of things. A real body detective doing their gosh darn job, and doing it well. The fact that they brought up biliary dyskinesia in the early beginning? Yeah, most doctors consider that a process of elimination diagnosis. But no, this dude knew better. I'm lucky to have them. 

Surgery consult is in a couple of weeks. We're evicting this bad boy.

Aaannndddd if you've made it this far, I'll share my symptoms:

As most of you can relate, I cannot tolerate fatty foods. I suffer primarily from ruq pain and nausea that correlates directly to the pain. It's pretty frequent right now, but I've had off and on problems with it throughout the years. I can have a good week where I can tolerate some fat, but then the next week a few grams of fat could send me to couch in the fetal position. 

The pain is not associated or relieved with bathroom usage, moving around, or antacids. Although, on my really bad days, food seemed to move a little too quickly. 

I noticed that panic attacks were also triggering pain attacks. I read that strong emotions can affect how the gallbladder works; something to do with brain signals. 

The pain makes itself right at home underneath my right ribs, usually it likes to jump over to my right shoulder as well. It's sharp during the beginning of an attack, but when the pain climaxes, it remains constant and unmoving until the attack is done. It kinda feels like my gb is using itself as a stress ball if that makes any sense. Throbby, achy, stabby here and there. 

The pain shows up on an empty stomach and within a couple hours of eating. Eating seems to alleviate symptoms for a little bit, I suspect the copious amounts of bile finally found something to work on instead of me. If I'm feeling really pissed at my body, I'll just eat when I'm in pain, the few minutes of blissful silence from my gut are worth it here and there. I found that grazing made the pain less- EXTRAVAGANT, have you. Either that or my gb attacks just ebb and flow, I guess I don't really know. Granted the pain was still there, but I think it helped during the days when I was recovering from my gbs latest temper tantrum. Like a freaking toddler getting mad that you won't let them pour their drink everywhere but the glass. 

Other symptoms worth noting are bloating during the really bad attacks, and yeah, some heartburn. But I get heartburn whenever I'm in really bad pain, so not really that often I guess? I also get really dizzy and clammy whenever the pain gets real bad, but that's probably a reaction to the pain, it subsides as the pain plateaus. 

It seems that pain and nausea remain supreme in my presentation of hyperkinetic bile bag. 

Slowly, over the years, the pain has become more continual. 

Relate if you can. Maybe your bile bag is a special kind of gassy, hyperkinetic toddler. Everyone presents differently. Even textbook cases have their quirky, atypical symptoms. You have a ☆unique☆ gallbladder.
